chunks: And Muḥammad ibn ‘ammad ibn ‘Abdillāh ibn Ja’far Al-Ḥimyari narrated to me from his father, from ‘Ali ibn Muḥammad ibn Sālim, from Muḥammad ibn Khālid, from ‘Abdillāh ibn Ḥammād Al-Basri, from ‘Abdillāh ibn ‘Abdil Raḥmān Al-Asam, from Ḥusain, from Al-Ḥalabi, from Abā ‘Abdillāh (peace be upon him), in a long hadith:

He said: I said, 'May I be sacrificed for you, what do you say about one who leaves his Ziyārah while he is able to do so?' He said: 'I say that he has disowned the Messenger of Allāh (peace be upon him) and disowned us, and he has belittled a matter that is obligatory on him.'
And whoever goes to his Ziyārah, Allāh will look after his needs, and he will be spared whatever concerns him from the affairs of his worldly life.
And verily it brings sustenance for the slave and compensates him for what he spent.
And He forgives him the sins of fifty years, and he returns to his family, and whatever burden or mistake is upon him has been erased from his record.
If he dies during his journey, the angels descend and perform his ritual bath, and the doors of Paradise are opened for him, and its fragrance descends upon him until he is resurrected.
And if he is safe (returns), the door from which sustenance descends is opened for him, and for every Dirham he spent, ten thousand Dirhams are made for him, and that is stored for him.
So when he is resurrected, it will be said to him: 'For you, for every Dirham, ten thousand Dirhams, and verily Allāh has kept it safely for you with Himself.'

key_terms.زِيَارَة: Ziyārah (visitation/pilgrimage to the shrine of an Imam or Prophet)
key_terms.عَقَّ: Disowned or neglected (in a relational context)

ai.seo_question: What are the rewards and consequences of performing the Ziyarah of Imam Husain?
ai.summary: In Kamil al-Ziyarat, Imam al-Ṣādiq (a.s.) elaborates on the profound spiritual and material blessings of Ziyārah, framing it as an act of loyalty to the Prophet and the Imams. The narration highlights specific rewards such as the forgiveness of fifty years' sins, divine protection from worldly cares, and a multiplier of sustenance, emphasizing that neglecting this duty while capable constitutes a form of 'disowning' (ʿaqq) the Ahl al-Bayt.
